chapters.name: Chapter 1: The farm as a business

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Keeping simple farm records
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Start a simple record of farm money in, money out and production.
This lesson builds toward: Using a notebook or phone spreadsheet, you will keep records of farm money in, money out and production, writing each item the same day, including family labour days.
You cannot manage what you do not measure. Many farmers know roughly what they spend and earn, but without records it is hard to see which crop pays, to plan, or to get a loan or a buyer contract.
Keep three simple records. Money out: date, what for (seed, fertilizer, labour, transport, vet), which crop or animal, amount. Money in: date, what you sold, how much, to whom, amount. Production: planting dates, inputs used, harvest per plot, eggs or milk per day. A notebook works; so does a phone spreadsheet. Mobile money statements also help you remember.
Write records the same day. Keep farm money separate from household money in your records, even if they come from the same pocket, and count family labour days too, because your time has value.
Step by step:
- Choose a notebook or phone spreadsheet.
- Make three pages or sheets: money out, money in, production.
- Record each item the same day: date, what, which crop or animal, amount.
- Use mobile money statements to fill gaps.
- Count family labour days as well as paid labour.
Words to know:
- Record keeping: writing down what happens on the farm: money, inputs and production.
- Enterprise: one activity on the farm, such as maize, beans, poultry or dairy.
Try it now: Start your records today. Make the three sheets and fill in at least five items from the last month from memory and your mobile money statement.
You can now keep simple records of money in, money out and production for each farm enterprise.

check.q: What are the three simple farm records in this course?
options: Money out, money in and production
check.why: These three records show what you spend, earn and produce.

check.q: You forgot to write last week's fertilizer purchase. What can help you remember?
options: Ask the AI to invent it
check.why: Mobile money statements help fill gaps in your records.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Gross margin: which crop pays best?
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate the gross margin per acre of two enterprises and compare them.
This lesson builds toward: Given yields, prices and variable costs, you will calculate the gross margin per acre of two enterprises and compare them, with correct math and risk and labour considered, not just the margin.
Gross margin = income from an enterprise minus the costs that belong to it (variable costs: seed, fertilizer, chemicals, hired labour, bags, transport). Work it out per acre (or per hectare, or per 100 birds) so you can compare enterprises fairly.
Example with made-up numbers in Kenya shillings, one acre each. Maize: 18 bags at 3,500 = 63,000 income; costs 34,000 (seed 3,000, fertilizer 14,000, labour 12,000, chemicals 2,000, bags and transport 3,000); gross margin 29,000. Beans: 5 bags at 9,000 = 45,000 income; costs 18,000; gross margin 27,000. The margins are close, but beans also add nitrogen and are harvested sooner. Use your own prices: they differ by place and season.
Also compare margin per day of labour and the risk: a crop with a high margin but a high chance of failure may not be the best choice. Fixed costs (land rent, tools, a water tank) are covered by the total of all gross margins.
Step by step:
- Pick two enterprises.
- Write expected yield and price per unit to get income.
- List variable costs for each.
- Gross margin = income - variable costs, per acre.
- Compare margin, labour and risk.
Words to know:
- Gross margin: income from one enterprise minus the costs that belong to it.
- Variable costs: costs that change with how much you grow, such as seed, fertilizer and labour.
- Fixed costs: costs that stay the same whatever you grow, such as land rent or a water tank.
Try it now: Calculate the gross margin per acre for two enterprises on your farm (or two you are considering) using your local prices. Which is higher, and which has more risk?
You can now calculate and compare gross margins to decide what to grow or keep.

check.q: Which is a fixed cost, not a variable cost?
check.why: A water tank is paid whatever you grow, so it is a fixed cost.

check.q: Tomatoes earn 50,000 per acre and cost 30,000 in variable costs. What is the gross margin?
check.why: Gross margin is income minus variable costs: 50,000 - 30,000 = 20,000.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Finding markets and better prices
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Compare at least three ways to sell and choose the best one for a crop.
This lesson builds toward: Given your main crop, you will compare at least three ways to sell and choose the best one, with prices from several buyers, the quality each needs, and any contract's terms in writing.
Prices often fall right after harvest, when everyone sells, and rise months later. Selling alone in small amounts to the first trader at the farm gate is easy but often pays least. Compare: local market, traders, cooperatives that bulk produce, processors and schools or hotels, contract farming with a buyer, and, where available, certified warehouses that store grain and may help farmers access credit against it.
Find price information: ask several buyers, check market price services and radio, and talk to your cooperative. Know the buyer's quality standard (moisture, grading, size, cleanliness) and meet it: clean, dry, sorted produce earns more and keeps longer.
Contracts can give a sure market, but read the terms: price or how it is set, quantity, quality standard, delivery dates, who pays transport, payment date and method, and what happens if the harvest fails. Get it in writing and ask your cooperative or extension officer to check it.
Step by step:
- List at least three ways to sell your crop.
- Get prices from several buyers and market information services.
- Learn each buyer's quality standard.
- Consider bulking with a group or storing for a better price.
- Read any contract's terms and get it in writing.
Words to know:
- Bulking: putting many farmers' produce together to sell larger amounts at better prices.
- Contract farming: an agreement to grow and sell produce to a buyer on set terms.
- Quality standard: the buyer's rules for moisture, size, grade and cleanliness.
Try it now: For your main crop, write three ways you could sell it, the price each would pay today (ask or estimate), the quality each needs, and which you will choose and why.
You can now compare markets and choose the best way to sell a crop.

options: Selling together as a group to get larger amounts
check.why: Bulking with a cooperative or group makes larger lots that can get better prices.

check.q: A buyer wants your beans but says nothing about when they will pay. What do you do?
options: Ask for the payment date and method in writing
check.why: A contract should set the payment date and method in writing.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Mobile money and cash flow
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan a 12-month cash flow and use mobile money safely for the farm.
This lesson builds toward: For the next 12 months, you will plan your farm's cash flow and use mobile money safely, marking the hungry months with a plan for each and never sharing a PIN or code.
Many farms have money problems not because they make a loss, but because money comes in once or twice a year and goes out all year. A cash-flow plan shows, month by month, money expected in and out, so you can see the hungry months coming and plan.
Mobile money (such as M-Pesa in Kenya, and mobile wallets and bank apps in Nigeria) makes it easier to pay workers and suppliers, receive buyer payments, save, and keep a record. Some farmers keep a separate wallet or account for the farm so farm and household money do not mix.
Stay safe: never share your PIN or one-time code with anyone, including people who say they are from the mobile money company or a buyer; check the name before you send; and be careful with unexpected "wrong transfer" messages asking you to send money back. Report problems to the provider through its official channels.
Step by step:
- Draw 12 month columns.
- Write expected money in each month (sales, other income).
- Write expected money out (inputs, labour, school fees, food).
- Find the months where out is bigger than in, and plan savings or timing.
- Use a separate wallet or account for farm money; never share your PIN.
Words to know:
- Cash flow: the timing of money coming in and going out.
- Hungry months: months when money or food runs short, often before harvest.
- PIN: the secret number that protects your mobile money account.
Try it now: Draw your 12-month cash-flow plan with money in and money out. Circle the hungry months and write one way to prepare for each (save from harvest, stagger sales, a small off-season enterprise).
You can now plan your farm's cash flow through the year and use mobile money safely.

check.q: What does a 12-month cash-flow plan help you see?
options: The hungry months before they come
check.why: It shows the months when money out is bigger than money in.

check.q: School fees are due in a month with no harvest sales. What is one way to prepare?
options: Spend all the harvest money at once
Take any loan offered by text
Save part of the harvest money or stagger sales
check.why: Saving from harvest or staggering sales covers the hungry months.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Credit and risk: borrowing wisely
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Work out the total cost of a loan and decide whether it makes sense for the farm.
This lesson builds toward: Given a loan offer, you will calculate the total cost of the loan and decide whether it fits your cash flow, adding every fee and checking the lender is licensed.
A loan can help buy inputs or equipment that earn more than they cost. It can also become a trap. Before borrowing, ask: what will the money buy, how much extra will it earn, and when? Will you be able to repay on the dates the lender sets, even if the harvest is poor?
Compare offers by the total amount you will repay, not just the interest rate: add all interest, fees and insurance charges. For example (made-up numbers), borrowing 20,000 and repaying 2,000 a month for 12 months means repaying 24,000: the loan costs 4,000. Check the repayment dates fit when your money comes in. Short digital loans can be very expensive when you add up the fees.
Use licensed lenders: banks, microfinance banks, SACCOs and cooperatives, and digital lenders approved by the central bank or the right regulator (in Kenya, the Central Bank of Kenya lists licensed institutions; in Nigeria, the Central Bank of Nigeria). Reduce risk with savings, diversified crops, insurance where available, and by borrowing only what the plan needs. Talk to a trusted adviser before signing.
Step by step:
- Write what the loan will buy and how much extra it should earn.
- Add up the total you will repay: interest, fees, insurance.
- Check repayment dates against your cash-flow plan.
- Check the lender is licensed.
- Plan for a bad season: savings, insurance, smaller loan.
- Ask a trusted adviser before signing.
Words to know:
- Interest: the price you pay to borrow money.
- Total cost of credit: everything you pay back above what you borrowed: interest plus fees and charges.
- SACCO: a savings and credit cooperative owned by its members.
- Collateral: something you promise the lender if you cannot repay.
Official sources:
- Central Bank of Kenya (see its lists of licensed institutions)
- Central Bank of Nigeria (consumer protection and licensed institutions)
Try it now: Take a real or example loan offer. Write the amount borrowed, every repayment and fee, the total repaid and the total cost. Then check the repayment months against your cash-flow plan and write whether it makes sense.
You can now work out the true cost of a loan and judge whether borrowing makes sense for your farm.

check.q: How should you compare two loan offers?
options: By the total amount you will repay, including all fees
By how fast the money arrives
check.why: The total repaid shows the true cost of each loan.

check.q: A loan's repayments start the month after planting, before harvest. What do you do?
options: Check it against your cash flow and ask for dates that fit when money comes in
Use your PIN to speed it up
check.why: Repayment dates should fit the months when your money comes in.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Writing a one-page farm business plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a one-page business plan you could show a cooperative, lender or partner.
This lesson builds toward: Using your records and numbers, you will write a one-page farm business plan with your main risks and how you will reduce them, with every required part and three goals with numbers.
A business plan is your farm's story in numbers and goals. Lenders, cooperatives, buyers and partners want to see that you know your farm, your market and your risks. One clear page is better than ten vague ones.
Include: who you are and your farm (location, land, what you produce); your enterprises with their gross margins; your market (who buys, how, at what price); your cash-flow outline; what you need (inputs, equipment, a loan) and how it will pay back; your main risks (weather, pests, prices) and what you do about them; and three goals for next season with numbers.
Keep your records and calculations behind the plan, so you can answer questions. Update it every season with what really happened.
Step by step:
- Farm summary: location, land, enterprises.
- Gross margins for each enterprise.
- Market: buyers, channel, price.
- Cash-flow outline and what you need.
- Risks and how you manage them.
- Three goals with numbers; update each season.
Words to know:
- Business plan: a short document that explains what a business does, how it earns, what it needs and its goals.
- Goal: a clear target with a number and a date.
Official sources:
- FAO: Climate-Smart Agriculture Sourcebook (farm risk management)
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page farm business plan with gross margins for two enterprises, market, 12-month cash flow, any loan and its total cost, risks and responses, and three goals for next season.
You can now write a one-page farm business plan backed by your own records and numbers.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Gross margins Fewer than two enterprises, or math errors. Gross margins per acre for two enterprises, with local prices and correct math. Compares labour and risk as well as the margin. Market No buyer or way to sell named. Names who will buy, how, and at what price. Compares at least three ways to sell and the quality each needs. Cash flow No month-by-month outline. A 12-month outline of money in and out, with hungry months marked. A plan for each hungry month. Loan A loan is listed without its total cost or repayment plan. Any loan shows the total repaid, total cost and how repayments fit the cash flow, or no loan is needed. Names a licensed lender and a plan for a bad season. Risks and goals No risks or goals. Main risks with how to reduce them, and three goals with numbers. Fits on one clear page backed by records. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Why keep records and calculations behind your one-page plan?
options: So you can answer questions about your numbers
check.why: Records back up your plan when a lender or buyer asks questions.

check.q: Your maize did worse than planned this season. What do you do with your business plan?
options: Update it with what really happened
check.why: A plan is updated every season with real results.
